newsitem.title: VATICAN: Netanyahu invites Pope, discusses fundamentalism.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu invites Pope, discusses fundamentalism.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed on Monday the dangers of Islamic fundamentalism on Middle East peace with Pope John Paul and invited him to make a historic visit to the Holy Land soon.
"We look forward to receiving you in Jerusalem," Netanyahu said as he left the Roman Catholic Pontiff's study after a 20-minute private audience.
The Polish Pope responded: "God Bless Israel".
No date for an eventual visit was given but a Vatican statement said Netanyahu had invited him "to make a pilgrimage to the Holy Land as soon as possible".
A senior diplomatic source said the Israeli leader, meeting the Pope for the first time, brought up the subject of how Islamic fundamentalism threatened Middle East peace efforts.
"He told the Pope: 'It's not rational, not in its cause, not in its method,'" the source said.
The Pope has condemned Islamic fundamentalist violence, most recently in Algeria, but also in the Middle East.
Netanyahu repeated an open invitation last made to the Pope in 1994 by the late prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.
Israeli army radio quoted Netanyahu as saying that the Pope told him that he wanted to visit the Holy Land before the year 2000, the start of Christianity's third millennium.
The Pope last year accepted an invitation by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to visit Christ's birthplace in Bethlehem at the turn of the millennium.
A trip to the Holy Land, one of the 76-year-old Pope's cherished dreams, would be the first by a Roman Catholic leader since Paul VI visited in 1964.

A Vatican statement said the Pope told Netanyahu he hoped it could be a place where "Jews, Christians, Moslems, Israelis and Arabs, believers and non-believers can create and consolidate a concrete peace in respect of everyone's rights and dignity".
The Vatican and Israel ended nearly 2,000 years of often hostile Catholic-Jewish relations in 1994 when they established full diplomatic relations.
The two sides have since been working towards agreement on issues regarding the legal status of the Catholic Church and its clerical hierarchy in the Jewish state.

The statement said Netanyahu promised the Pope "to move ahead along the same path" as his predecessors towards reaching an agreement on the legal status of the Catholic Church in the land where Christ lived and died.
The Vatican statement did not say whether the two had discussed the divisive issue of the status of Jerusalem, which Israel declared its "united and eternal capital" in 1980.
The Vatican, which like most other countries keeps its embassy in or near Tel Aviv, wants international guarantees protecting Jerusalem as sacred for Christians, Moslems and Jews.

Arafat said during a visit to Rome last year that Jerusalem would either make or break Middle East peace. Palestinians view East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Six-Day War, as the capital of a future state.

The Pontiff, who has suffered a string of health problems over the last few years, appeared in good form during the picture-taking session of the audience. He joked and chatted easily with Netanyahu, his wife Sara and their delegation.
